2027-06-09.title: Fourth Wednesday of the Apostles · Mar Aprem (St Ephrem the Syrian)
2027-06-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: You shall be a people holy to the Lord your God
Moses, whose memory is blessed: the law of life and knowledge
God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit
You are the salt of the earth and the light of the world
2027-06-09.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Mar Aprem (St Ephrem the Syrian) is listed in the First Set calendar as an important feast, with the readings above. Weekday readings of the Fourth Wednesday of the Apostles: 1 Corinthians 15:31–34; Matthew 14:22–33. In the Latin calendar St Ephrem, deacon and Doctor of the Church, is an optional memorial on the same day. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-09.verse: You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.
theo: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian, whom the Syriac tradition calls “the Harp of the Spirit”. For the Syro-Malabar Church he is not a distant figure. He is one of the fathers of our own Syriac heritage: his hymns and his way of praying shaped the liturgy of the Church of the East, from which our Holy Qurbana, our Hours and our feasts have come down to us. Ephrem was born around the year 306 in Nisibis, a frontier city between the Roman and Persian empires, in what is now south-eastern Turkey. He grew up in the Christian community of that city, was formed by its bishop, Mar Jacob of Nisibis, and served the Church as a deacon and a teacher. When Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363, Ephrem went with the Christians who left the city and settled in Edessa (Urhai), where he taught and wrote for the last ten years of his life. Tradition says that he died in 373, after spending himself in caring for the hungry and the sick during a famine. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the universal Church.

Ephrem was a theologian who sang. He wrote verse homilies (memre), commentaries on Scripture, and above all hundreds of madrashe, teaching hymns set to melodies that the people knew. He trained choirs of women to sing them in the church, so that the faith of Nicaea, the mystery of the Incarnation, the virginity of Mary and the gift of the sacraments would be carried in the memory and the heart of ordinary believers. He did not reduce God to definitions. He knew that God is beyond our grasp, and that the best way to speak of him is often through the symbols that God himself has placed in Scripture and in nature: the pearl, the light, the fire, the bread, the robe, the womb, the river. His hymns teach us to stand before the mystery with wonder rather than curiosity, with love rather than argument. That is why the Church calls him a Doctor: not only because he taught truly, but because he taught us how to adore.

The readings of his feast are well chosen. Sirach praises Moses, “whose memory is blessed”, whom the Lord “allowed to hear his voice, and led him into the dark cloud, and gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, so that he might teach Jacob the covenant, and Israel his decrees.” Ephrem too entered the cloud of the divine mystery and came back to teach. Deuteronomy calls Israel “a people holy to the Lord your God”, a treasured people set high “in praise and in fame and in honor”. Ephrem's hymns are one long effort to make the Church that holy, praising people. And Paul gives the source of it all: “hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.” In this Season of the Apostles, after Pentecost, we see in Ephrem what the Spirit does when he is poured into a heart: he turns it into an instrument of praise, a harp on which the Spirit himself plays.

The Gospel is from the Sermon on the Mount: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.” Jesus adds a word that fits a teacher of the Church: “whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” Ephrem did not only teach; he lived what he taught. He remained a deacon, a servant, all his life, and his last work was not a hymn but the care of the hungry in a time of famine. His light shone through good works, “so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.” His love for Mary was tender and strong; he sang of her as the one who carried the Fire that does not burn, and he could say to Christ that he and his Mother alone are entirely beautiful, without any stain (in substance). In his hymns on the Eucharist he marvels that the Spirit and the fire dwell in the bread and in the cup, and that we eat and drink the Lord himself.

The weekday readings add their own note. Paul says, “I die every day!”, and asks the Corinthians to come “to a sober and right mind”, because the dead will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:31–34). In the Gospel Jesus walks on the water, and Peter, sinking, cries out, “Lord, save me!” (Matthew 14:30). Ephrem's life, lived on a troubled frontier, through sieges, exile and famine, was a long walk on the water, held by the hand of Christ. He invites us today to sing our faith, to love the liturgy we have received, to teach it to our children, and to let the Holy Spirit make each of us a harp in the hands of God.
conn: Face to face, as with a friend.
“Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11); Sirach 45:5 recalls the dark cloud and the law of life.
“Awake, my soul! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn” (Psalm 108:2): the psalmist's harp becomes Ephrem's name, the Harp of the Spirit.
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God” (Colossians 3:16).
Moses saw a bush that burned without being consumed (Exodus 3:2); Ephrem and the Syriac tradition see in it Mary, who carried the divine Fire without being consumed.
Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and to his disciples, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14): the saints shine with a borrowed light.
“But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19): Ephrem learned from her to ponder the mysteries and to sing them.
altar: Mar Aprem marvelled that in the bread of the Qurbana there dwells the Spirit who is not consumed, and in the cup the Fire that is not drunk (in substance). At this altar we receive the living Christ himself. Let us receive him with Ephrem's wonder, and let our thanksgiving become a hymn.
The Holy Qurbana we celebrate in the Syriac tradition carries the voices of Ephrem and of the fathers who prayed before us. Let us pray it with understanding and love, and hand it on to our children.
outline: A deacon of Nisibis and Edessa who taught the faith in song: the Harp of the Spirit.
Point 1 · God's love poured into our hearts
The Spirit turns a heart into a harp.
Entering the cloud of mystery and coming back to teach the law of life.
A theology lived in service, to the last day of famine.
Mary, the Eucharist and the liturgy we have received.
Women's voices in the church of Edessa singing the faith of Nicaea to a melody everyone knew.
“You are the light of the world.”
live: Learn by heart one hymn of the Holy Qurbana or the Hours this week, and sing it at home.
Explain to a child or a young person one part of the Qurbana: why we stand, why we face the east, why we sing.
Do one hidden good work this week for the hungry or the sick, as Ephrem did in the famine.
Spend five minutes each day this week pondering one mystery of the Rosary in silence.
fathers: You alone, Lord, and your Mother are fair in every way; for in you there is no blemish, and in your Mother no stain.
In your bread is hidden the Spirit who is not eaten; in your wine dwells the Fire that is not drunk. The Spirit in your bread, the Fire in your wine: a wonder, received by our lips.

Lord, who can grasp even one of your words? We leave behind far more than we take from it, like thirsty people drinking from a spring. Let the thirsty one rejoice that he drank, and not grieve that he could not drink the spring dry.
St Ephrem shows that theology can be done in poetry; his hymns combine faith and beauty, and teach that the mystery of God is best approached through praise.
magis: The musical tradition of the universal Church is a treasure of inestimable value; song and music are integral to solemn liturgy.

Song and music fulfil their function as signs more significantly the more closely they are connected with the liturgical action: beauty expressive of prayer, the unanimous participation of the assembly, and the solemn character of the celebration.

The liturgical traditions or rites presently in use in the Church include the Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian or Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite and Chaldean rites; the Church holds all of them to be of equal right and dignity.
Address one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with all your heart: the hymns of the Church are an expression of the praise of God.
saints: Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon, teacher of Nisibis and Edessa, the Harp of the Spirit, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1920; an important feast in the First Set calendar. In the Latin calendar, an optional memorial on the same day.

7–12 June: the fourth week of the Season of the Apostles. Tue 8: St Mariam Thresia, the saint of the families of Kerala (an important feast). Wed 9: Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian, the Harp of the Spirit (an important feast; in the Latin calendar an optional memorial the same day). Thu 10: Fourth Thursday of the Apostles. Fri 11: St Barnabas, the Apostle (in the Latin calendar a memorial the same day). Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles; St Antony of Padua, so dear to Kerala, gives way to the Sunday this year. June is the month of the Sacred Heart, and in Kerala the month of the monsoon and of the new school year.
2027-06-09.prayer: Lord God, you poured your love into the heart of Mar Aprem through the Holy Spirit and made him a harp of praise, a teacher of the true faith and a servant of the hungry. By his prayers, give us hearts that sing your wonders, minds that ponder your mysteries with humility, and hands that serve the poor. Make our families and parishes love the holy liturgy we have received from our fathers; keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles; and with the Virgin Mary, whom he praised so tenderly, let us glorify you in the Church, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

quick: Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian, deacon and Doctor of the Church, taught the faith through hymns: the Harp of the Spirit.
Sirach: Moses taught the law of life; Paul: God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
Jesus: you are the salt of the earth and the light of the world; whoever does and teaches the commandments will be called great.
2027-06-09.action: Learn one hymn of the Holy Qurbana by heart this week and sing it at home.
2027-06-09.question: Does my faith sing, or has it become only a duty?
catechism: The liturgical traditions of the Church, the Syriac among them.
kidsaint: Ephrem lived long ago in a city called Nisibis, and later in Edessa. He was a deacon and a teacher. He loved Jesus and Mother Mary so much that he wrote hundreds of songs about them, and he taught choirs to sing them in church, so that everyone could learn the faith by singing. People called him the Harp of the Holy Spirit. When there was a famine, he took care of hungry and sick people. Lesson: we can praise God with our voices and with our hands!
2027-06-09.special: Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian (important feast). Fourth Wednesday of the Apostles.
term: A Syriac teaching hymn, sung in stanzas to a known melody with a refrain. Mar Aprem wrote hundreds of madrashe on faith, the Nativity, the Church, Paradise and the sacraments, and had them sung by choirs so that the faithful would learn true doctrine by heart. The Syriac liturgical tradition of our Church still sings hymns in this spirit.

family.explain: Jesus says that we are the light of the world. A lamp is not hidden under a basket; it is put on a stand so that it gives light to everyone in the house. Mar Aprem was a light because he sang about God and helped the poor. When we sing in church, pray together and help others, our light shines and people praise God.
family.intention: We pray for choirs and all who sing in church, for catechism teachers, and for families who are hungry.
family.ask: Ask: “Which hymn from church do we love most? Can we sing it together tonight?”

illus: A young man from a parish in Changanacherry went to study engineering in Germany. In his first months he stopped going to church; the language was strange and he felt alone. One Sunday, homesick, he searched on his phone for a recording of the Holy Qurbana in Malayalam and played it in his room. When the choir sang a hymn his grandmother used to sing in the kitchen, he found himself in tears. The next week he looked for the nearest Syro-Malabar community, two hours away by train, and went. Later he wrote to his parish priest: ‘I forgot many things I learned in catechism, but I never forgot the songs. They brought me back.’ Mar Aprem, who taught the faith through melodies, would not have been surprised.

pm.open: Holy Spirit, you made Mar Aprem a harp of praise. Tune our hearts to your melody, open our minds to the word, and let our lives give glory to the Father. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us. Amen.
share: God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). When did I last feel this love and praise God for it?
He gave him the commandments face to face (Sirach 45:5). Do I listen to God's word as Moses listened?
You are the light of the world (Matthew 5:14). Where is my light hidden under a basket?
Whoever does them and teaches them will be called great (Matthew 5:19). Do I practise what I teach my children?
pm.resp: Lord, make us a harp of your Spirit.
interc: For the Church, that her liturgy may be beautiful and her faith sung with joy.
For the Syro-Malabar Church and all the Churches of the Syriac tradition, that they may treasure their heritage.
For choirs, musicians and catechists, that they may teach the faith through beauty.
For those who suffer famine, war and exile, as Ephrem did.
For young people far from home, that the songs of faith may lead them back to Christ.
pm.close: Lord God, you raised up Mar Aprem to sing your mysteries and to serve the poor. By his prayers, make our lives a hymn of praise and a light for others. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian. He was born around the year 306 in Nisibis, served as a deacon and a teacher, and spent his last years in Edessa. He died in 373, and the Church declared him a Doctor of the Church. The Syriac tradition calls him “the Harp of the Spirit”.

Ephrem taught the faith in a special way: he sang it. He wrote hundreds of hymns, set them to tunes the people knew, and trained choirs to sing them. In this way ordinary people learned the truth about Jesus, about Mary and about the sacraments, not only in their heads but in their hearts.

Saint Paul tells us where such praise comes from: “God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). When the Spirit fills a heart, it begins to sing. Ephrem's heart became a harp, and the Spirit played on it.

Sirach praises Moses, to whom God spoke face to face, who received “the law of life and knowledge” in order to teach the people (Sirach 45:5). Ephrem too entered the mystery of God in prayer and came back to teach. He did not try to explain God away; he stood before God with wonder and love.

In the Gospel Jesus says: “You are the salt of the earth… You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:13–14). Ephrem's light shone not only in his hymns but in his service. At the end of his life, during a famine, he cared for the hungry and the sick.

Our Church has received the Syriac liturgy that Ephrem helped to shape. Let us love it, pray it with understanding, and teach it to our children. Let us sing our faith, and let our good works give glory to our Father in heaven. Mar Aprem, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, Mar Aprem loved Jesus so much that he wrote songs about him, hundreds of songs! He taught people to sing them in church, so that they could learn about God by singing.
When you sing in church, sing with your whole heart, because singing is praying twice. And like Mar Aprem, help someone who is hungry or sad. Then your light will shine for Jesus!

intro: Theme: “You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.”
On the feast of Mar Aprem: the Harp of the Spirit, the teacher who entered the cloud like Moses, and the light of a theology lived in service.

points.h: A harp in the hands of the Spirit
sub: God's love poured into our hearts.
Praise as the fruit of Pentecost.
q: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast; I will sing and make melody. Awake, my soul! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
points.apply: Begin each day this week with one verse of a psalm or hymn sung, not only said.

points.h: A teacher who entered the cloud
sub: Moses, face to face with God.
q: He allowed him to hear his voice, and led him into the dark cloud, and gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, so that he might teach Jacob the covenant, and Israel his decrees.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
points.apply: Teach a child one hymn or one part of the Holy Qurbana this week.

q: My heart overflows with a goodly theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe.
In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.
points.apply: Do one hidden work of mercy for the hungry or the sick this week.

concl: Mar Aprem shows what the Spirit does in a heart: he makes it sing, teach and serve.
Let us love the Syriac heritage we have received, sing our faith, and let our light shine in good works.
2027-06-09.resolve: This week, sing one hymn at home each day, teach one part of the Qurbana to a child, and do one hidden work of mercy.
